History:
• Chief complaint: Progressive upper lip swelling beginning ~30 min after eating prawn soup at 19:00 today.  
• Course: Swelling started at left lip corner, now involves entire upper lip and “getting bigger.”  
• Associated symptoms: Difficulty breathing, possible chest tightness, dizziness. No explicit throat pain but feels throat “closing up.”  
• Past similar episodes:  
  – Age ~6: Hospitalized for severe allergic reaction (details unknown).  
  – 1 yr ago after late-night Chinese meal: Woke with facial swelling and breathing difficulty; self-managed with salbutamol.  
• Triggers: Prawn soup today; known peanut allergy.  
• No mention of rash, abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma.  
• Peanut allergy (history of anaphylaxis).  
• No other chronic illnesses reported.

Allergies:
• Peanuts – history of severe reaction.  
• Shellfish allergy not previously documented; suspected today.

Medications:
• Salbutamol inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Antihistamines (unspecified) PRN – currently none available.

Physical Examination:
(telehealth observation)  
• Visible upper-lip swelling.  
• Patient appears distressed, reports dyspnea and dizziness.  
• Speech coherent; able to answer questions.  
• No other findings provided (vital signs, skin rash, wheeze, etc., not assessed).  
• Alert and oriented ×3.

Impression:
Suspected acute anaphylactic reaction (likely shellfish-induced).

Management Plan:
• Immediate activation of emergency services (999) for transport to ED.  
• Advised on-site caregiver to administer available oral antihistamine while awaiting ambulance.  
• Remain with observer until EMS arrival.  
• Post-hospital: contact clinic for further allergy management and consideration of epinephrine auto-injector prescription.

Patient Summary:
Maria developed rapid lip swelling, breathing difficulty, and dizziness ~30 min after eating prawn soup, consistent with an evolving anaphylactic reaction. EMS has been called, antihistamine advised, and she will be taken to hospital for definitive care.

Key Takeaways:
• Call 999 immediately with any signs of throat swelling or breathing difficulty.  
• Take an oral antihistamine as soon as possible while awaiting help.  
• Follow up after hospital discharge to arrange long-term allergy management and an epinephrine auto-injector.

Next Steps:
• Emergency department evaluation and treatment (likely epinephrine, airway support, observation).  
• Formal allergy referral/testing for shellfish.  
• Prescription and training for epinephrine auto-injector.  
• Update asthma and allergy action plans.
